beads.title: Accept disco from any of a peer's known disco keys, and switch the active key on receive
beads.description: Upstream gives each magicsock endpoint two disco-key slots with an origin each -- the key control sent (controlKey) and the key the peer advertised over TSMP (tsmpKey) -- plus a tsmpActive flag choosing which one is sent to. At commit 9ea7cba44591e0cd840c6c94d23274dd222059bf every inbound disco comparison in Conn.handleDiscoMessage and unambiguousNodeKeyOfPingLocked goes through endpoint.checkAndUpdateDiscoKey, which accepts EITHER slot's key and, when the key seen is the currently-inactive one, compare-and-swaps tsmpActive so that key becomes active and calls changedActiveDiscoLocked. A peer that told us K2 over TSMP but is still sending disco under the K1 control gave us is therefore understood, and we switch to K1 for sending because that is demonstrably what the peer uses. This repository already mirrors the two-slot model: ts_runtime::peer_tracker's EndpointDisco has control, tsmp, tsmp_active and the key() / key_from_control() / key_from_tsmp() accessors, each cited to its Go name. What is missing is the ingress half. PeerDb stores exactly one disco_key per node -- the effective key EndpointDisco::key() -- and indexes only that one (disco_idx in ts_runtime/src/peer_tracker/peer_db.rs); ts_runtime::direct::DiscoPeerLookup resolves an inbound frame's sender key through that single index. A frame arriving under the peer's OTHER known key resolves to no peer and is silently dropped, and there is no recovery except waiting for control or for another TSMP advertisement. Against a real Go peer mid-rotation that is lost direct connectivity, falling back to DERP. The decision to make is where the second key becomes reachable for attribution: widen the disco index so both a peer's keys resolve to it (and decide what happens when two peers transiently claim the same key, which peer_db already has a regression test for), or resolve ingress through EndpointDisco and leave the index carrying only the effective key. Whichever is chosen, the active-key switch and the path-invalidation it triggers must happen on the same code path, and the negative case -- a key belonging to NEITHER slot is still refused -- has to be asserted, because that refusal is the whole security value of the check. Land this before the sibling item about control no longer preempting an active TSMP key: making TSMP sticky without first accepting ingress under the control key would strand a peer whose key control has legitimately rotated. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.

beads.title: Stop a control disco-key update from preempting an active TSMP-learned key
beads.description: At the previous pin, Go's endpoint.updateDiscoKey set epDisco.tsmpActive = false whenever control supplied a non-zero disco key, so control changing its mind always took the active slot back. At commit 9ea7cba44591e0cd840c6c94d23274dd222059bf that line reads epDisco.tsmpActive = old.tsmpActive || key.IsZero(): control's new key is still recorded in its slot, but a TSMP-learned key that is already active STAYS active, and the switch back to control's key happens only when disco is actually received under it (via endpoint.checkAndUpdateDiscoKey). The same upstream commit routes TSMP-learned keys straight into the engine rather than through controlClient, and replaces the full peer reconfigure on a key change with wireguard-go's ScheduleHandshakeOnUserSend optimistic handshake. This repository still implements the old rule: EndpointDisco::update_from_control in ts_runtime/src/peer_tracker/mod.rs does self.tsmp_active = key.is_none(), handing the active slot back to control on any real control-side change. The doc comment on PeerTracker::upsert_from_control asserts 'Control genuinely changing its mind still wins, exactly as it does upstream' -- true at the previous pin, false at this one, and the most misleading line in the tree on this subject; fix the comment with the code. The decision to make is the ordering, and it is not optional: this must land AFTER the sibling item that accepts disco under either of a peer's known keys. Making TSMP sticky first would leave us sending to a key the peer has legitimately rotated away from with no ingress path to notice. The ScheduleHandshakeOnUserSend half has no target here -- ts_tunnel is this fork's own WireGuard implementation and exposes no such callback -- but nothing regresses by omitting it, because this tree does not tear down and re-establish the peer on a disco-key change either. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.

beads.title: Invalidate the trusted direct path when a peer's disco key changes
beads.description: Upstream sets trustBestAddrUntil = 0 and calls invalidateDiscoPathLocked() on every disco-key transition -- control-side in endpoint.updateFromNode, TSMP-side in Conn.HandleDiscoKeyAdvertisement, and on an active-slot switch in endpoint.checkAndUpdateDiscoKey, all three funnelled through changedActiveDiscoLocked at commit 9ea7cba44591e0cd840c6c94d23274dd222059bf. bestAddr itself is deliberately KEPT so data keeps flowing while a fresh path is confirmed; only the trust window and the path-discovery state are reset. Upstream restored this after an earlier commit removed it, with the stated reason that otherwise the node coasts on a dead path until trust lapses on its own. This repository has the right primitive and never calls it from here. ts_magicsock::path::PeerPaths::invalidate_best (ts_magicsock/src/path.rs) drops the confirmed best and its trust while keeping the candidate set -- exactly Go's shape -- but its only caller is MagicSock::rebind (ts_magicsock/src/sock.rs), and its doc comment says so. Nothing on the disco-key change path invokes it, so after a peer rotates its disco key this node keeps trusting a best that was confirmed by a pong signed under the OLD key for up to a full TRUST_DURATION (6.5s) before re-probing. The decision to make is where the hook goes given this fork's actor split: the disco key changes in ts_runtime::peer_tracker, while the trust window lives in ts_magicsock::path, so the invalidation has to cross that boundary (the published PeerState snapshot is the existing channel). Test the positive case (trust dropped, re-probe scheduled) and the negative one that gives the change its value: best itself is NOT cleared, so traffic keeps flowing over the old address until a new pong lands. Independent of the two multi-key disco items; can land before or after either. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.

beads.title: Withhold routes and peer capabilities from UnsignedPeerAPIOnly peers
beads.description: At commit 9ea7cba44591e0cd840c6c94d23274dd222059bf upstream refuses network access and capabilities to peers control marks UnsignedPeerAPIOnly, on the stated grounds that such peers are outside tailnet lock's coverage and so 'a (possibly malicious) control server must not grant them network access via advertised routes'. Three sites: upgradeNode in control/controlclient/map.go clamps such a node's AllowedIPs back to its own Addresses; nodeBackend.peerCapsLocked / PeerCapsForIP / PeerCapsForService in ipn/ipnlocal/node_backend.go return nil for them; and nodeHasCap in wgengine/magicsock/magicsock.go refuses them the relay allocation/target capabilities. All three are UNCONDITIONAL -- they do not depend on tailnet lock being enabled. Here the field is decoded and then dropped. ts_control_serde::Node carries unsigned_peer_api_only (ts_control_serde/src/node.rs), but ts_control::Node has no such field, so no consumer downstream can see it; the peer-trust chokepoint in ts_runtime/src/peer_tracker/mod.rs says as much in a comment ('no UnsignedPeerAPIOnly exemption (our node model lacks the field)'). With tailnet lock ACTIVE this tree is stricter than Go, rejecting unsigned peers outright -- docs/PARITY_ROADMAP.md records that as a deliberate divergence in the safe direction. With tailnet lock OFF, which is the default and the common case, there is no clamp at all: control can hand an unsigned peer 0.0.0.0/0 in its allowed IPs and this node will route to it. That is the case upstream closed, and it is NOT the roadmap's deferred item -- the roadmap entry is about admission under an active lock, this is about routes and capabilities with the lock off. The decision to make is how far to carry the field. The minimum faithful port is the upgradeNode clamp: thread unsigned_peer_api_only onto ts_control::Node and clamp accepted_routes / allowed IPs to the node's own addresses when it is set. The peer-capability half needs a prior decision that is already recorded as open in ts_runtime/src/peerapi.rs ('thread PeerCapMap into ts_control::Node'), and may reasonably be split out. Test the clamp with a peer that advertises a route AND is unsigned (route dropped) alongside one that advertises the same route and is signed (route kept), so the test cannot pass by dropping routes generally. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.

beads.title: Attach an SOA to negative MagicDNS answers and cut the positive TTL to 5 seconds
beads.description: At commit 9ea7cba44591e0cd840c6c94d23274dd222059bf upstream's MagicDNS resolver attaches the zone's SOA record to the authority section of every NXDOMAIN and NODATA response it is authoritative for (marshalSOA / response.SOAZone in net/dns/resolver/tsdns.go), advertising a 10-second negative-caching TTL per RFC 2308, and lowers defaultTTL for positive answers from 600 seconds to 5. All SOA fields other than the TTLs are placeholders -- nothing consumes the serial (no secondaries, no zone transfers), so it is the response time in unix seconds. The motivating bug is concrete and reproduces off-tailnet: macOS mDNSResponder caches an SOA-less negative answer on its own schedule, so a name queried shortly BEFORE a node was renamed to it does not start resolving until something flushes the cache. The 600 -> 5 change is the same argument in the positive direction -- the source of truth is local and in-memory, so re-queries are nearly free, while a downstream cache delays clients noticing a rename for the full TTL. This repository has neither half. ts_dns_wire's ANSWER_TTL is still 600 (ts_dns_wire/src/lib.rs), and neither ts_dns_wire::encode_response nor ts_runtime::magic_dns ever emits an authority section -- responses are header, question and answers only. The negative answers this affects are the ones this node generates authoritatively: a tailnet-suffix name with no peer, a CGNAT reverse lookup that misses the peer set, a NODATA for a qtype served authoritatively but absent. The decision to make is how much SOA machinery to add to a hand-rolled wire encoder that currently has no RR types beyond A/AAAA/PTR: the record is fixed-shape and its variable fields are placeholders, so a single encode_soa helper is likely enough, but the zone name has to be chosen (upstream uses the authoritative zone containing the question, which here is the matching search domain). Note the interaction with the existing 512-byte authoritative cap in ts_dns_wire and with set_tc_if_over_client_limit: adding an authority record makes a previously-fitting negative answer larger, so the truncation path needs a test with the SOA present. Host-facing, not wire-facing. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.

beads.title: Offer every checkpoint ancestor in a TKA SyncOffer instead of an exponential sample
beads.description: At commit 9ea7cba44591e0cd840c6c94d23274dd222059bf upstream's Authority.SyncOffer no longer samples ancestors at exponentially increasing intervals. The ancestorsSkipStart = 4 / ancestorsSkipShift = 2 constants are gone; the walk now appends every ancestor whose MessageKind is AUMCheckpoint, and maxSyncHeadIntersectionIter in tka/limits.go rose from 400 to 1000. The reason is a real failure mode rather than tidiness: nodes compact aggressively (last 24 AUMs, everything from the last two weeks, then back to the last checkpoint) and may hold only ~50 AUMs, so an exponentially sampled offer can be DISJOINT from what the node kept. The node then cannot find a common ancestor, enters a poll-and-fail loop, and carries an increasingly stale view of the tailnet indefinitely. Every node is guaranteed to keep at least one checkpoint after compaction, which is precisely why checkpoints are the right thing to offer. ts_tka::Authority::sync_offer (ts_tka/src/lib.rs) still implements the superseded algorithm exactly, constants and all: ANCESTORS_SKIP_START = 4, ANCESTORS_SKIP_SHIFT = 2, MAX_SYNC_HEAD_INTERSECTION_ITER = 400, each cited by name to the Go constant it mirrors. This is control-observable: the offer is what this node sends control during /machine/tka/sync. The decision to make is how far to follow. The mechanical part -- walk parents, push a hash when message_kind is the checkpoint variant, raise the cap to 1000 -- is small and self-contained. The trap is that sync_offer's output is also consumed locally by missing_aums, which builds a local offer and runs intersection against the remote one; both the head-intersection and tail-intersection arms need re-checking against an ancestor list that is now checkpoints-only rather than a dense-then-sparse sample. Test with a chain long enough that the old sampling and the new checkpoint list actually differ, and assert the case the change exists for: a local chain compacted back to one checkpoint still finds an intersection with a far-ahead remote offer. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.

beads.title: Drop host-injected TSMP on the TUN-to-WireGuard path
beads.description: Upstream's filterPacketOutboundToWireGuard in net/tstun/wrap.go drops any packet the host writes into the TUN whose IPProto is TSMP, counting tstun_out_to_wg_drop_tsmp, on the rule that TSMP traffic 'should only originate from tailscaled, not from the host itself'. The same function has long dropped host-originated disco packets for the same reason (the issue 1526 workaround, tstun_out_to_wg_drop_self_disco). Both refusals are present at commit 9ea7cba44591e0cd840c6c94d23274dd222059bf. This repository has no outbound protocol filter at all. ts_dataplane::process_outbound (ts_dataplane/src/lib.rs) tees to the capture hook, routes by destination through or_out.route, encrypts and sends; nothing inspects the IP protocol on the way out. In TUN transport mode a local process that writes an IP-proto-99 packet addressed to a peer therefore gets it delivered. That matters more here than it would have a year ago: this node now has a real TSMP disco-key advertisement sender, so a forged advertisement from the host is indistinguishable to the peer from one this node meant to send, and can make the peer bind a disco key of the attacker's choosing for us. The decision to make is where the check goes and what else joins it. The natural site is the top of process_outbound, before or_out.route consumes the packets -- but note that the TSMP messages this node legitimately sends are injected BELOW that point via the wireguard priority-message path, so the drop must not reach them; a test asserting that our own advertisements still go out is the negative case that keeps this fix from silently disabling capability version 144. Whether to port the self-disco drop in the same change is a judgement call: it is the same one-line shape in the same function upstream, but it is a separate refusal with its own metric, and the repository's quality bar prefers one coherent slice per PR. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.
